did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter says that during the Assyrian campaign, in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib captured all the fortified cities of Judah.
Did you know? The Rabshakeh was sent from Lachish to Jerusalem at the head of a large army and took up his position by the channel of the Upper Pool, on the road to the Washerman’s Field.
Did you know? Three of Hezekiah’s officials went out to meet the Rabshakeh: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace; Shebna the secretary; and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder.
Did you know? The Rabshakeh compared reliance on Egypt to leaning on a broken reed: anyone who leans on it may be injured, just as a broken staff can pierce the hand.

Did you know? The Rabshakeh presented Hezekiah’s removal of the high places and altars as evidence against the king’s confidence, even though Hezekiah had sought to centralize the worship of the LORD in one place.
Did you know? Hezekiah’s officials asked the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, which they understood, rather than in Hebrew, so that the people on the wall would not understand what he was saying.
Did you know? The Rabshakeh refused the officials’ request, stood up, and shouted loudly in Hebrew, directing his message straight to the people of Jerusalem on the wall.

Did you know? The Rabshakeh offered the people of Jerusalem the chance to surrender, leave the city, and each eat from his own vine and fig tree and drink from his own cistern until they were taken to a land like their own.

Did you know? To undermine the people’s confidence, the Rabshakeh mentioned Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, and Samaria, claiming that the gods of those nations had not saved their lands from the king of Assyria.

Did you know? Hezekiah’s officials did not answer the Rabshakeh because that was the king’s command. Then they returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him what the Rabshakeh had said.
